title: One request, start to finish
dek: When a customer opens a restaurant in the Zotato app, a dozen messages cross the network before the menu appears: a name is looked up, a connection is opened and secured, the request goes out, and later the connection is closed. Counting those round trips explains most of what makes an app feel fast or slow.

items: A fresh request costs a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake before the request itself: up to four round trips before the first byte of the answer.
Round trips, not bandwidth, decide how fast most API calls feel. On a phone each one costs tens of milliseconds.
So reuse connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2), cache DNS answers, and make fewer, larger requests. A connection is state on both ends, which matters once you keep many of them open.

body.cap: Seen from the wire, one menu request is four exchanges: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP. The server's 40 ms of work is the only part most engineers measure, but on a phone the round trips before and after it are often larger.

items: DNS. The phone needs an address for api.zotato.in. It asks a resolver (usually run by the mobile network or a public service), which may ask further servers and then answers with 13.235.4.20 and a time to live, say 60 seconds. Phone and resolver both cache the answer, so later lookups are usually free.
TCP handshake. The phone sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the phone sends ACK. Both sides now have state for this connection: sequence numbers, buffers, timers. One round trip.
TLS handshake. Phone and server agree encryption keys and the phone checks the server's certificate for api.zotato.in. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip; the older TLS 1.2 needed two.
The request. GET /menu/42 goes out, the server reads the database and builds the menu, and the response comes back: 200 OK with 18 KB of JSON, in one round trip plus the server's own time.
Closing. Either side sends FIN, the other acknowledges and sends its own FIN, which is acknowledged too. In practice apps keep the connection open and close it only after it has been idle a while.

body.x: Every layer and every box in the path adds its own share: a load balancer in front of the servers is one more hop, an API gateway another, each with its own connections to open. Each costs little alone, which is why it's easy to ignore until a page needs ten calls in a row and the small costs add up.

A request is many packets, not one. The 18 KB response is about a dozen packets of 1,500 bytes; each is acknowledged; any lost one is resent. It is easy to forget, and it is why a design that 'makes one call' may still be slow on a poor network.

body.x: Multiply: on 4G at 60 ms a round trip, a cold request with DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP takes about 240 ms before the server's own work is even counted. The same request on a warm connection takes 60 ms.

body.cap: The same three requests cost 9, 5 or 3 round trips depending only on how connections are used. Nothing on the server changed.

items: Keep-alive: HTTP/1.1 keeps a connection open after a response so the next request can use it. Browsers and mobile HTTP libraries do this by default; make sure your servers and load balancers don't close idle connections too eagerly.
HTTP/2 sends many requests at once over one connection, each as its own stream, and compresses headers. A home screen that needs ten calls no longer opens six connections.

Connection pools between your own services: an app server keeps, say, 20 open connections to the database and lends them out per query. Opening a fresh database connection can take several milliseconds; a pooled one costs nothing.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (on UDP), which merges the transport and TLS handshakes into one round trip, and can resume a known server with zero.

body.x: Every open connection holds memory and a file handle on the server, and an entry in each load balancer and NAT on the path. A server can hold tens of thousands of idle connections comfortably, but not unlimited numbers, and a connection that is kept open to push live updates ties the client to one particular server. That is why designs with long-lived connections (live order tracking, chat) need extra thought: which server holds a user's connection, what happens when it restarts, and how a message for that user finds it. The articles on pushing updates and on load balancers in Networking essentials come back to this.

items: When latency matters, count round trips, not bytes: 'a cold call from a phone in India to a US region costs nearly a second before any work is done'.
Mention connection reuse and pooling when you draw service-to-service calls and database access. It's a cheap, credible optimisation.
'What happens when you type a URL' is asked less often now, but walking through DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP and rendering in two minutes is still a good warm-up.
`curl -v https://example.com` prints each stage as it happens: the address it resolved, the TLS handshake, the request headers it sent and the response headers it got back.
`dig api.example.com` shows a DNS answer and its TTL; run it twice and watch the TTL count down from the cached copy.

In the browser's developer tools, the Network tab breaks every request into DNS, connecting, TLS, waiting and download. Turn on throttling (for example 'Slow 4G') and reload: the handshakes, not the downloads, take most of the time.
`traceroute` (or `mtr`) lists the routers between you and a server and the round trip to each, which shows where distance is spent.
Wireshark captures the packets themselves: the SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK, the TLS hello, retransmissions on a bad network.
HTTP/1.1 is plain text, so you can even type a request by hand: `nc example.com 80`, then `GET / HTTP/1.1`, `Host: example.com` and an empty line.

To feel a bad network on purpose, add delay and loss: Apple's Network Link Conditioner (part of Xcode's extra tools) on a Mac or iPhone, or `tc netem` on Linux. Try your own app on a poor 3G profile and watch what it does when calls stall.

body.label: Go deeper: why a new connection is slow even after the handshakes

body.x: TCP doesn't know how much the network between two machines can carry, so a new connection starts cautiously: it sends about ten packets (roughly 14 KB) and waits for acknowledgements before sending more, doubling the amount each round trip while nothing is lost. This is called slow start.

So a 100 KB response on a fresh connection takes three or four round trips to arrive, even on a fast network, while the same response on a warm connection arrives in one. It is another reason to reuse connections, and a reason to keep the first screen's responses small.
